opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is really about scale, both in terms of compute and in terms of people.

When I first joined NVIDIA, around ten years ago, research was much more of an individual or small-team activity. You had an idea, maybe you worked with one or two interns, you had a handful of GPUs, and in a few months you could write a paper. A lot of the generative work we did back then, the early GAN-based image translation work, for example, was done that way. The ambition was bounded by what a small group could do with modest resources. You picked problems where a clever idea could make a difference without needing enormous infrastructure.

Over the years, especially in the last three or four years, the nature of the problems changed. If you want to build something like a world foundation model, a model that can understand and simulate the physical world for robotics or autonomous driving, you can't do that with three people and eight GPUs. You need large-scale data curation pipelines, thousands of GPUs, people who are experts in tokenizers, in diffusion, in autoregressive models, in systems and infrastructure, in evaluation. It becomes much more like an engineering project combined with research.

So for me, the change in ability came from a few things. First, the company itself grew, and the importance of AI to NVIDIA became much more central, so leadership was willing to invest in bigger bets. Second, I personally grew from being an individual researcher into someone leading a team, and I had to learn how to organize people around a shared goal rather than just my own ideas. And third, over ten years you build trust. When you've delivered a few times, people are more willing to give you resources to try something bigger.

I would say the mindset also changed. Earlier, the question was "what is a good paper I can write?" Now the question is more "what capability does the world need, and what does it take to build it?" That's a very different kind of ambition. It's less about novelty for its own sake and more about whether this thing can actually be used by developers, by robotics companies, by people building physical AI. That shift, from papers to platforms, is probably the most important change in how I think about research.

r001.rationale: He describes becoming able to pursue larger projects through NVIDIA’s increased investment, his growth into a team leader, and the trust earned by delivering. This frames the change as greater capacity to execute ambitious research.

r002.rationale: He says AI became more central to NVIDIA and leadership was willing to invest in bigger bets, but does not identify demonstrating the importance of a particular research decision to the company as a way to influence investment.

fable-5.1.text:
When I joined NVIDIA in 2016, it was still a company that most people associated with gaming GPUs, and the research group was small. I remember my early projects were very much about proving that a thing could work at all. Image-to-image translation, pix2pixHD, GauGAN. We would train on a handful of GPUs, and the ambition was limited by what you could fit in a lab. The question I asked myself was not "what is the most important problem in the field," it was "what interesting problem can I actually finish with what I have."

What changed over ten years is that the ceiling moved, and it moved in a way that was tied to the company itself. As NVIDIA became the infrastructure for all of AI, the people inside the company started getting access to that infrastructure early. So the scale of what I could attempt grew with the scale of what the company was building. Around 2020, 2021, with the diffusion work and then large generative models for video, I began to notice I was no longer choosing problems by feasibility. I was choosing them by whether they mattered.

But I want to be honest about the other side of this. More resources do not automatically make you more ambitious. They can make you more conservative, because the cost of failure is visible. When ten GPUs fail, nobody notices. When ten thousand GPUs run for months and produce nothing, people notice. So I had to actively relearn how to take risks. The thing that helped me was being clear with leadership, and with Jensen, that research means some fraction of what we do will not work, and that this is the price of doing something new rather than something safe.

The other change is that I stopped thinking of myself as an individual researcher. In my first years, the ability to do ambitious work was mostly my own skill and time. Now it is about building a team that can carry a multi-year vision, like what we are doing with Cosmos and world foundation models for physical AI. The ambition lives in the group, not in me. My job became less about having the idea and more about creating the conditions where a hundred people can pursue one very large idea together without losing the willingness to be wrong.

So if I summarize it, the first five years taught me how to do research with constraints. The second five years taught me how to stay a researcher when the constraints disappeared. The second one was harder.

r001.rationale: The response describes his capacity to attempt larger research growing with NVIDIA’s infrastructure, shifting from choosing feasible projects to choosing consequential ones.

r002.rationale: It says he explained to leadership why research requires accepting failures, but does not say he demonstrated a research decision’s importance to the company to influence investment.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is in the scale of the problems I feel comfortable taking on. Earlier in my career, I would think about what I could accomplish myself, or with a few collaborators. Now I think more about what a team can accomplish together, and what we need to build to make an ambitious idea possible.

That doesn’t mean the research becomes easy. You still don’t know whether an idea will work. But you become more comfortable with that uncertainty. You learn how to break a big question into smaller experiments, learn from the results, and decide when to keep pushing or change direction.

So, for me, the change is less about becoming a better individual researcher and more about becoming better at enabling research—bringing people together and giving an ambitious idea room to develop.

r001.rationale: The response describes becoming comfortable taking on larger problems and better at enabling a team to pursue ambitious research, framing the change as increased ability to carry it out.

r002.rationale: It does not mention demonstrating a research decision’s importance to the company or using that to influence company investment.

sol-6.1.text:
Over those ten years, I think the biggest change has been the scale of the questions I feel able to take on. Earlier, I was more focused on whether I could get a particular idea to work and turn it into a strong research result. As I gained experience, I became more comfortable pursuing a longer-term direction where the path wasn’t clear at the beginning.

That’s also about the people around you. Ambitious research takes more than an individual idea—you need collaborators who bring different strengths, resources to test your assumptions, and enough trust to work through failures. For me, growing as a researcher means getting better at bringing those pieces together, while still being willing to question my own ideas.

r001.rationale: The response describes becoming more able to pursue larger, longer-term research questions with uncertain paths, framing the change as increased capability rather than increased ambition.

r002.rationale: It does not mention showing that a research decision matters to the company or using that to influence company investment.
